Physiology of Sleep Apnea
In this video, we'll dive more into understanding why OSA, or obstructive sleep apnea, happens. In OSA, your throat relaxes so much that it narrows and/or creates a blockage during sleep, leading to difficulty breathing. (Imagine sucking air through a straw and then pinching the straw.) Your brain senses the lack of oxygen and wakes you up just enough to breathe (though you might not remember it). In OSA, these interruptions happen many times a night, leading to poor sleep quality. Over time, this repeated strain stresses your body causing poor quality of life.

Apnea and Hypopnea
You may hear two terms when discussing a sleep study: • Apnea means airflow stops or nearly stops for a period of time.
• Hypopnea means airflow becomes partly reduced. The image compares typical breathing with obstructive sleep apnea. With typical breathing, the airway stays open so air can move past the tongue and soft palate. In OSA, those tissues narrow or block the airway, so airflow is reduced or stops even though the person is still trying to breathe. Both apnea and hypopnea can disturb sleep and may affect oxygen levels. A sleep study measures breathing events and other information to help a clinician understand what is happening during sleep.

What are the symptoms of sleep apnea?
OSA does not feel the same for everyone. Possible nighttime signs include loud snoring, pauses in breathing noticed by another person, gasping, choking, frequent awakenings, or restless sleep. Possible morning or daytime experiences include dry mouth, headache, tiredness, difficulty concentrating, irritability, or feeling unrefreshed after sleep. Having one of these symptoms does not by itself prove that someone has OSA.

Symptoms can raise concern for sleep apnea, but they cannot confirm it on their own. Studies show individual with partners actually experience better CPAP adherence, meaning your partner can help keep you accountable! To some couples, it may seem like CPAP is an intimacy barrier, but it is integral for a patient with sleep apnea to use the machine, especially when pregnant. Untreated sleep apnea can have drastic effects on both the mother and the baby, as we learned in the previous modules.

Establishing a Good Sleep Routine Part 2: Sleep/Wake Times
The second component of a good sleep routine is keeping the same bedtime and wake times. Wake up around the same time each morning and go to sleep around the same time at night—even if you didn't sleep well the night before. This anchors your body's internal clock (circadian rhythm), and can help you be more tired at night (especially if you didn't sleep well the night before). This applies especially for the weekends! It may be tempting to sleep in on the weekends, but when you shift your sleep schedule back and forth on the weekends (called social jet lag), it's similar to your body crossing time zones on a weekly basis. The third component of a good sleep routine is avoiding blue light before bedtime. Blue lights (and bright lights in general) inhibit your body's production of the sleepy chemical (melatonin), which is great in the morning when you want to wake up, but is detrimental at night when you want to feel tired. Most electronic devices these days emit lots of blue light, which is why scrolling on your phone before bed is very bad for your sleep. Instead, here are some changes to your routine that can help you feel more tired at night and improve sleep quality: • Keep the lighting at home to a minimum before bedtime. Dim the lights around the house, and when light is still needed, switch to warmer hues (orange/red). • Use night shift/color filters on your phone and reduce the brightness. The best solution would be to not use your devices close to bedtime. Night shift can make your phone emit less blue light at night or turning on a red color filter can completely eliminate blue light emission from your phone.

What should you do if you have trouble falling asleep? Having trouble falling asleep may happen around pregnancy. If having trouble falling asleep last for more than 20 minutes, the best thing you can do is to get out of bed, go to another room, and engage in a quiet and relaxing activity in low-light conditions, such as reading, listening to calming music, or practicing meditation. You would want to associate the bed with sleep; so getting out of the bedroom when you are not feeling sleepy helps maintain that association. Only return to bed when you feel sleepy. What you should NOT do if you're having trouble falling asleep is using electronic devices. Electronic devices can signal to your brain to stay awake for longer. Do NOT engage in stimulating activities, like reading a thriller or listening to loud music. Do NOT turn on bright lights in the middle of the night, as that can mess up your ability to fall back to sleep. Do NOT check the time, as this can increase anxiety and frustration around sleep.

Chrononutrition (Meal Timing for Sleep)
Chrononutrition refers to how meal timing can affect your sleep and circadian rhythm. Let's look at some of the best chrononutrition advice. Front-load your calories and hydration earlier in the day. “Eat breakfast like a king, lunch like a prince, and dinner like a peasant.” • Your body processes food best earlier in the day (the food is more likely to be used for fuel rather than fat). • Your body also feels fuller from the same meal if eaten earlier in the day due to better hormonal signaling and metabolism. This means that eating a big breakfast, then shifting lunch and dinner earlier in the day, could help you feel fuller, with fewer cravings at night. • Consider eating lunch and dinner earlier in the day, finishing your last meal 4–5 hours before bedtime for sleep and general health. • Early hydration helps prevent you from having to pee at night, which pregnant women are more susceptible to since the baby can compress the bladder, and because overall blood volume is higher. Try to avoid big meals at least 3–4 hours before bed. • This helps prevent your body from having to actively digest food while trying to sleep at the same time, which can worsen sleep quality. • Arguably, finishing your last meal even farther from bedtime (5+ hours) is even better, since your resting heart rate will drop, which is a very strong indicator of sleep quality.

entries.approved_text:
Nasal Congestion
Background Nasal congestion from pregnancy rhinitis (nasal inflammation) is very common, with some reviews reporting it in up to 42% of pregnancies. It is also common for nasal congestion to get worse later in pregnancy. Causes and Complications Body–fluid changes and pregnancy hormones like estrogen and progesterone can all cause the lining of the nose to swell, which can make breathing through the nose harder and cause women to feel congested. This nasal congestion can disrupt sleep, and as the nose is part of the airway, nasal congestion can exacerbate snoring, and worsen sleep apnea. Addressing nasal congestion may help breathing during sleep. Nasal congestion can also impact how well people tolerate the CPAP mask. As the CPAP device blows air through the mask (whether it is a nasal mask, a full face mask, or nasal pillows), nasal congestion often makes CPAP more uncomfortable and may increase leak through the mouth. However, this can be addressed to improve comfort.

Nasal Congestion Treatment
When using PAP, consider turning on the heat and/or humidifier elements to help prevent dryness and nasal irritation during sleep. Besides that, nasal sprays are a great low-risk solution for nasal congestion. Consider starting with a simply saline spray before bed. Saline spray or foams can be purchased over the counter and help reduce congestion. They consist of salt and water and are safe to use in pregnancy. If symptoms persist, intranasal steroid sprays such as Fluticasone, or budesonide, which may be purchased over the counter, can be considered. These nasal sprays are also considered safe to use in pregnancy. Possible side effects include nasal dryness, stinging/burning, throat irritation, or nosebleeds, but are usually mild. When using nasal sprays, and after placing the spray inside your nose, make sure to point the tip of the nasal spray outwards towards your eyes and not straight up the nose, to target the outer lining. In case you have nasal congestion that is related to a cold or upper respiratory infection, you may use a topical decongestant sprays such as Afrin, but do not use it for more than 2–3 days. When used for a longer period of time, this type of nasal spray may cause rebound congestion and tends to worsen symptoms.

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
Background Symptoms of GERD (such as heartburn) during pregnancy are very common, with studies reporting a prevalence of 30–80%. This condition also often worsens later in pregnancy. Causes and Complications Pregnancy can relax the muscle tone in the lower esophageal sphincter (the muscle that normally keeps stomach contents in the stomach). This lower tone can increase the likelihood of stomach contents, including the acid produced by the stomach, going back up the esophagus. This can cause common symptoms such as heartburn, regurgitation, a sour taste in the mouth, or nausea. OSA and GERD can both individually worsen sleep quality. In addition, OSA may worsen GERD, as when you try to inhale with a blocked airway, a suction-like negative pressure can pull stomach contents upward into the esophagus.

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) Treatment
The best first-line treatments for GERD and heartburn are usually dietary changes and bed adjustments, such as: • smaller meals with reduced fat content of meals • less caffeine (for example coffee, tea, coke or pepsi, energy drinks.) • Finishing your last meal 3–4 hours before bedtime • Consider avoiding common trigger foods, such as fatty fried foods, spicy foods, tomato, citrus, or carbonated drinks. • Elevating the head of the bed 6–10 inches (this can be done by using a wedge pillow or even putting books under the head of the bed frame). Elevating just your head with pillows does not necessarily change stomach positioning. • Sleeping on your left side • Antacids If lifestyle modifications aren't enough, acid-reducing medicines such as H2 blockers (famotidine, nizatidine, cimetidine) or proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) can be considered during pregnancy. These medications are generally safe and have been shown by the literature to not be the cause of birth defects, but consult with your doctor before starting one of these medications.

Anxiety
Background Symptoms of anxiety during pregnancy are very common, with studies reporting a prevalence of ~20% of pregnant women meeting the criteria for an anxiety disorder and with higher rates based on symptoms. Causes and Complications Pregnancy brings about rapid physical, hormonal, and emotional changes, in addition to uncertainty of the future, which can exacerbate feelings of stress. These factors, along with worsened sleep quality from untreated OSA may lead to higher levels of anxiety. Regarding PAP, anxiety can exacerbate a claustrophobic feeling from the mask, which can cause people to take off overnight or use it less overall. Helpful strategies to getting accustomed to the mask can include trying different mask styles, practicing wearing the mask while awake, using relaxation breathing, or adjusting the humidity and ramp settings.

How does sleep apnea impact my sex life?
During pregnancy, it is very normal for sex drive to change due to body changes, discomfort, stress, or fatigue. Sleep apnea itself can reduce your sex drive. This is primarily because sleep quality is worsened, which can lead to: • Less energy and desire • Hormone disruption • Increased stress, anxiety, or depression • Reduced blood flow When wearing CPAP, it can be normal to have a negative body–image perception, which can sometimes decrease sex drive. However, CPAP plays a crucial role in improving sleep quality for individuals with OSA, which can help restore energy, desire, blood flow, and reduce feelings of stress/anxiety.
